risks.description: [dynamodb] Flagged by the Aurora PostgreSQL analysis for 1 query now on DynamoDB: High-frequency reads of small, rarely-changing data (config, sessions, feature flags). Aurora serves them natively from memory once read (MySQL Reference Manual, Buffer Pool; PostgreSQL documentation, Resource Consumption, shared_buffers), so a cache in front is a latency choice. (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 1 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Cover the 1 remaining query in the DynamoDB schema design or route it to an engine that serves it.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Full-text search patterns using LIKE '%term%' or similar constructs. Guidance only: the scan an unindexed substring match needs is priced once, as its own pattern, and a word search is not penalised (PostgreSQL documentation, pg_trgm). (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 3 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Load-test the text search in the 3 flagged queries on Aurora PostgreSQL with production-scale data and review its text index and search configuration where latency or result quality misses the target.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Table with no foreign keys and no join participation: all queries are single-table CRUD. Aurora serves single-table CRUD natively and uses none of its relational features for it (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora). (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 2 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Load-test the 2 flagged queries on Aurora PostgreSQL with production-scale data before cutover and tune indexes or query plans where the measured latency misses the target.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Table accessed by at most 2 distinct query patterns, all single-table, all by primary key or single column filter. Aurora serves these reads natively and its query optimizer adds nothing to them (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora). (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 2 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Load-test the 2 flagged queries on Aurora PostgreSQL with production-scale data before cutover and tune indexes or query plans where the measured latency misses the target.

risks.description: [dynamodb] A write wider than one transaction: more than 100 items, or rows a range, join, subquery or a filter with no key anchor picks (a write by a non-unique key column is a key-scoped Query plus batch write, not this). DynamoDB TransactWriteItems holds up to 100 items and 4 MB across tables (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Amazon DynamoDB Transactions). (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 1 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Writes of up to 100 known items run as one TransactWriteItems call. A wider write needs batches of at most 100 items or a retry-safe multi-step flow.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] 3 queries use a leading-wildcard LIKE or a regular expression on Aurora PostgreSQL: SELECT r.[ReviewID], r.[Rating], r.[Title] FROM [ProductReview] r WHERE r.[Prod…; SELECT TOP (10) [ArticleID], [Title] FROM [KnowledgeArticle] WHERE [Body] LIKE…; SELECT TOP (24) [ProductID], [Sku], [Name] FROM [Product] WHERE [Name] LIKE '%'…. Aurora PostgreSQL indexes a leading-wildcard LIKE and a regular expression with a pg_trgm trigram index (GIN or GiST), an extension to create (the PostgreSQL documentation of pg_trgm describes its index support for LIKE, ILIKE, ~ and ~*). 3 of them are word searches.
risks.mitigation: Create the pg_trgm extension and a GIN trigram index on the column (CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm), which serves this LIKE, word searches included; full-text search (to_tsvector) also ranks word matches.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Not checked: schema design was not run for DynamoDB, so 6 queries assigned to it have no access pattern to check against: INSERT INTO [Audit].[PriceChangeLog] ([ProductID], [OldPrice], [NewPrice], [C...; SELECT [BrandID], [Name], [Country] FROM [Brand]; SELECT [FlagKey], [Enabled], [Rollout] FROM [FeatureFlag]; and 3 more
risks.mitigation: Run the DynamoDB schema design; any of these queries it does not serve then becomes a schema design gap.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 32 reads run on a copy of 17 tables that CDC keeps in sync from Aurora PostgreSQL and DynamoDB across 2 engine pairs, so a read there can miss a recent write. 5 more tables are read here and written by no captured query, so a one-time copy serves them.

Compare the row counts on both sides at the Wave 3 gate.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 21 queries were decided by less than 5 points: 13 go to DynamoDB over Aurora PostgreSQL and 8 stay on Aurora PostgreSQL over DynamoDB. A small change in the scores moves them.
risks.mitigation: Confirm the engine for these queries in the assignment review before Wave 3 starts, using the close calls section; move any that fit the runner-up better.

migration_waves.title: Move off SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL (cross-engine)
migration_waves.rationale: The source SQL Server database (15.0.4322.2) has no Aurora engine of its own dialect: Aurora MySQL and Aurora PostgreSQL both competed on the collected workload, and the assignment resolver selected Aurora PostgreSQL to serve it. Aurora MySQL scored 7251.0 and Aurora PostgreSQL 7281.0 in total adjusted query fit; tipped by JSON usage, MERGE statements, multiple schemas, sequences. This is a cross-engine move: SQL dialect and schema conversion, not a 1:1 carry-over. 47 queries (49.5%) remain on Aurora PostgreSQL once later waves have moved their share; later waves move subsets of these 31 tables and views out of Aurora PostgreSQL.
migration_waves.gate: Cross-engine move: validate the schema and query translation to Aurora PostgreSQL (SQL dialect and data model conversion, not a 1:1 carry-over) before cutover.

migration_waves.title: Cache hot reads with ElastiCache
migration_waves.rationale: 16 hot reads (73.1% of calls), cache-aside in front of Aurora PostgreSQL in wave 2, then DynamoDB once wave 3 moves these reads: no data migration, fully reversible. It takes the read pressure off before the data migrations that follow. These reads belong to queries that move in wave 3 (DynamoDB) and wave 1 (Aurora PostgreSQL); this share overlaps the owner shares, which alone sum to 100%.

migration_waves.rationale: 48 key-value and point-lookup queries (50.5% of query patterns) across 1 table group, where co-dependent tables move together: the pattern DynamoDB fits best, and the smallest-blast-radius data migration available once the cache wave has absorbed the read pressure.

gaps.feature: APPLY joins and OPENJSON or OPENXML
gaps.reason: CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY become LATERAL joins, and OPENJSON and OPENXML become the target's JSON or XML table functions (jsonb_to_recordset or JSON_TABLE).
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation), JSON and XML

gaps.feature: T-SQL string, null and other built-in functions
gaps.reason: These T-SQL functions have other names on the target, and ISNULL exists on Aurora MySQL with a different meaning, so each call is converted (COALESCE, LENGTH, POSITION, gen_random_uuid() or UUID(), COUNT).
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation), String functions; AWS Schema Conversion Tool User Guide

gaps.reason: T-SQL date functions have other names or argument orders on the target, and DATEDIFF exists on Aurora MySQL with a different meaning, so each call is converted.
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation), Date and time functions

gaps.reason: TOP (n) becomes LIMIT n, and a DELETE or UPDATE with TOP becomes a keyed subquery.
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation); AWS Schema Conversion Tool User Guide

gaps.reason: T-SQL routines are converted to the target's procedural language (PL/pgSQL on Aurora PostgreSQL, stored programs on Aurora MySQL): a schema conversion tool converts most of the code, and the rest is rewritten by hand.
gaps.docs: AWS DMS User Guide, Converting database schemas using DMS Schema Conversion; AWS Schema Conversion Tool User Guide

gaps.reason: SQL Server compares text case-insensitively under its default collation, and Aurora PostgreSQL compares case-sensitively unless a column uses citext or a nondeterministic ICU collation, so lookups, sorts and unique keys on text can change.
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation), Collations

gaps.reason: PostgreSQL 15 and later run MERGE, with differences from T-SQL: INTO is required, and the OUTPUT clause becomes RETURNING (PostgreSQL 17), so check each statement.
gaps.docs: PostgreSQL documentation, MERGE; SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation)

gaps.reason: Neither target has T-SQL table or query hints, so they are dropped: readers never block writers under the targets' multi-version concurrency, so NOLOCK's dirty reads go away.
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation), Query hints and table hints

gaps.reason: These types map to the nearest target type: datetimeoffset keeps the instant but not the original offset, money becomes numeric(19,4), and bit becomes boolean (Aurora PostgreSQL) or BIT(1) (Aurora MySQL), so check the code that compares or formats them.
gaps.docs: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL Migration Playbook (AWS DMS documentation), Data types

gaps.reason: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL accepts T-SQL and SQL Server's wire protocol (TDS), which can keep much of this code unchanged: check its list of supported features before planning a full conversion.
gaps.docs: Amazon Aurora User Guide, Working with Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL

gaps.reason: These types are converted to the target's matching type (for example nvarchar to varchar in UTF-8, datetime2 to timestamp, tinyint to smallint on Aurora PostgreSQL): check precision and range in the conversion report.
gaps.docs: AWS Schema Conversion Tool User Guide, data type mappings
